quote: Then there’s only a constant complexity penalty to design your own universal Turing machine
content: For a fixed pair of universal machines the constant is fixed. Solomonoff's convergence theorem bounds the mixture's total expected prediction error by a quantity proportional to the complexity of the true environment, on any universal machine (Solomonoff 1978, IEEE Transactions on Information Theory; Rathmanner & Hutter 2011). Choosing a perverse machine buys a larger bound, never a failure to converge. Leike and Hutter's bad priors concern AIXI's exploration as an agent acting in the world, not sequence prediction, which is this essay's subject (Leike & Hutter 2015). Sterkenburg's circularity charge is a live philosophical dispute, but it does not touch the theorem that any reasonable choice of machine washes out.

quote: It’s enormously easier (as it turns out) to write a computer program that simulates Maxwell’s equations, compared to a computer program that simulates an intelligent emotional mind like Thor.
content: A frontier language model is a few hundred lines of code plus hundreds of billions of learned parameters, trained on trillions of words of human output. A Maxwell solver is a page of code and a handful of constants. The note concedes that the weights must be counted, and once they are, the comparison the essay makes comes out in its favor by a factor of about a billion. Boundary conditions cancel, because both Thor and Maxwell must be told where this particular storm's charge sits. What differs is the law, and for a law covering every thunderbolt ever observed, the short program wins by every measure the essay names.

quote: The complexity of anger, and indeed the complexity of intelligence, was glossed over by the humans who hypothesized Thor the thunder-agent.
content: That agency detection explains Thor is the essay's own claim: "If anger seems simple, it's because we don't see all the neural circuitry that's implementing the emotion." The note says agency detection is "over-applied to weather, illness and noises in the dark," which concedes that a prior centered on the human brain gives systematically wrong answers about the physical world. That is the reason not to use the cortex as the reference machine for physics: its built-in hypotheses were fitted to other minds, and the weather is not a mind. The Turing machine is chosen because it has no such built-in favorites, which is the property a prior over the world's laws needs.

The essay says the same thing about the witch: "The real sneakiness was concealed in the word 'it' of 'A witch did it.' A witch did what?" A specified witch theory that compresses 0101 passes the essay's criterion, and the razor cuts only the unspecified one, exactly as the note concludes. On phlogiston, the essay's claim is that it was used as an account that fitted anything after the fact. That is Lavoisier's complaint, that the principle "adapts itself to all the explanations for which it may be required" ("Réflexions sur le phlogistique," 1785, no DOI).
